result.paraphrase: Identifying aesthetic highlights is difficult when trying to understand the affective processes that occur while watching films. In this article, we examine spectators’ reactions to movie aesthetic stimuli in a social setting and seek to uncover the emotional component of aesthetic highlights in films. Our premise is that during these highlights, spectators’ physiological and behavioral responses become synchronized because (i) filmmakers’ aesthetic decisions are intended to evoke specific emotions, such as special effects or empathy and compassion toward a character, and (ii) watching a film together synchronizes spectators’ affective reactions through emotional contagion. We compare several methods for estimating synchronization across multiple spectators’ signals, including pairwise, group, and overall synchronization measures, to detect aesthetic highlights in movies. The results indicate that an unsupervised architecture based on synchronization measures can capture different aspects of spectators’ synchronization and identify aesthetic highlights using both electrodermal and acceleration signals. We find that pairwise synchronization measures are the most accurate, regardless of highlight category or movie genre. We also observe that electrodermal signals are more discriminative than acceleration signals for highlight detection.
